x: The Pandya capital Madurai stands on the Vaigai, the Pandya lifeline; the option printed here as 'Vengi' is a misprint of Vaigai (Vengi is the Eastern Chalukya region, not a river). The Godavari, Krishna and Tungabhadra are Deccan rivers.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval India Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-03.txt) p.32 (Pandyas: capital Madurai, port Korkai); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaigai_River (Madurai on its banks; Pandya fish emblem legend)

x: Chandragupta II is the first Gupta emperor whose genuine records and coins call him Parama-bhagavata (PMF; Epigraphia Indica 26). Samudragupta gets the title only in the Nalanda and Gaya copper plates, which are held to be later forgeries.
source: PMF Ancient & Medieval India Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-ancient-medieval-03.txt) p.65 (Chandragupta II adopted Parama-bhagavata); Epigraphia Indica Vol. 26 p.175 https://jainqq.org/pagetext/Epigraphia_Indica_Vol_26/032580/175 ('Chandragupta II the first Paramabhagavata among the Gupta emperors')
dispute: Official key / most books: Chandragupta II. The Rocket sheet gives Samudragupta, from the Nalanda and Gaya plates, which Epigraphia Indica 26 treats as forgeries copying his successors' epithets.

from_notes: Ramappa temple, a symbol of Kakatiya architecture, was built during his reign.
x: The Ramappa tank and temple at Palampet were built in 1213 by Recherla Rudra during Ganapatideva's reign, so the pond belongs to Ganapatideva's time. Rudradeva, Mahadeva and Prataparudra are wrong.
source: NextGen AP History - Kakatiyas (src/ap-history/nextgen-08-kakatiyas.txt) p.33 (Ramappa temple built by Recherla Rudra 1213), p.51 (built during Ganapatideva's reign), p.63 (Ramappa Pond); NextGen AP History 08 (src/ap-history/ap-history-appsc-08.txt) p.21 ('Racharla Rudra built Ramappa Tank')
dispute: Key / most books: Ganapatideva (the ruling king). Strictly: the tank was built by his general Recherla Rudra in 1213 (NextGen AP History 08 p.21; Kakatiyas p.33); Recherla Rudra is not an option.

from_notes: The Muslim King Ulumkhan held Pratapa Rudra as hostage.
from_notes_src: NextGen AP History previous papers (src/ap-history/nextgen-previous-papers.txt) p.58
x: In the final invasion of 1323 Ulugh Khan (Prince Juna Khan, later Muhammad bin Tughlaq) defeated Prataparudra II and took him captive; he died on the Narmada on the way to Delhi. Malik Kafur's 1309-10 siege ended in a treaty.
source: NextGen AP History - Kakatiyas (src/ap-history/nextgen-08-kakatiyas.txt) p.19 (Ulugh Khan, 1323), p.57-59 (Juna Khan defeated and captured Prataparudra); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_bin_Tughluq ('also known as ... Jauna Khan, Juna Khan or Ulugh Khan')
dispute: Key: Ulugh Khan (the usual name in keys). Juna Khan, also printed, is the same man (Muhammad bin Tughlaq), and NextGen Kakatiyas p.59 uses that name, so both options are strictly right.

x: Dakhili troops were raised by the state and placed under the mansabdars. Walashahi (Balashahi) was the emperor's bodyguard. (The stem's 'not paid directly by the state' is the question's wording; Wikipedia's Mansabdar article says they were state-paid.)
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansabdar ('The dakhili foot were paid by the state but handed over to the umara'); old app notes 1:133 (old-notes.txt) sub 2
dispute: Key: Dakhili (UPSC 2003). Strictly: dakhili troops were paid by the state and only placed under the mansabdars (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansabdar), so the stem's 'not paid directly by the state' is loose.

x: Many books and keys name 'Ustad Isa' as the Taj's chief architect, so the key is Ustad (Khalil) Isa; modern scholarship credits Ustad Ahmad Lahori (from his son Lutfullah Muhandis's writings), with Isa at most a draftsman.
source: PMF Art & Culture 04 (src/indian-history/pmf-art-culture-04.txt) p.6 (Ustad Ahmad Lahori, principal architect); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ustad_Ahmad_Lahori (Ustad Isa story from 19th-century informants)
evidence: app notes 1:137 (sub 5: chief architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori)
dispute: Most books and keys: Ustad Isa. Strictly: Ustad Ahmad Lahori was most likely the principal architect, and the Ustad Isa story comes from 19th-century informants (PMF Art & Culture 04 p.6; Wikipedia 'Ustad Ahmad Lahori'). Ahmad Lahori is not among the options.

x: The fort at Machilipatnam (Bandar Kota) was built by the Dutch, who set up their first factory there in 1605 (NextGen). The year 1611 belongs to the English (British) factory opened after the Globe arrived. The English built no fort there in 1611.
source: NextGen Powerplay Medieval 09 (src/ap-history/powerplay2-medieval-09.txt) p.5 ('Dutch also reached Masulipatnam and built a fort there'); NextGen Modern India L2 Part 1 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-01.txt) p.10 (Dutch factory 1605; British factory 1611 by Hippon); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Coromandel ('Dutch-built Bandar Fort')
evidence: https://vedantu.com/question-answer/the-fort-of-masulipatnam-was-built-by-the-a-class-7-social-science-cbse-5fc9e2b4455060145fdff2f1 (Class 7 question: fort built by the Dutch)
dispute: Printed key / books: the Dutch built the Masulipatnam fort. Strictly, 1611 is the year of the English factory (Globe, Hippon), not of any fort; no source dates the fort to 1611.

x: Shiv Dayal Singh, a Khatri (Soamiji Maharaj), founded the Radhasoami Satsang at Agra in 1861, drawing on Sikh scriptures. The stem's 'Sikkim, 1851' is garbled (Sikhism, 1861); the other names are unrelated.
source: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) pdf p.257 (Shiv Dayal Saheb, Agra, 1861); Rocket Indian History 02 (src/indian-history/rocket-indian-history-02.txt) p.80; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiv_Dayal_Singh (Sahejdhari Khatri family)
dispute: Key: Shiv Dayal Khatri. The stem's 'born out of Sikkim in 1851' is garbled: the Satsang began at Agra in January 1861 (Wikipedia 'Radha Soami'; Spectrum).

x: Kudi Arasu, the Tamil weekly that Periyar launched at Erode, became the organ of the Self-Respect Movement (PMF: Periyar started Kudi Arasu, Puratchi and Viduthalai). It was launched on 2 May 1925, not 1924.
source: PMF Modern History Part 5 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-05.txt) p.126; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kudi_Arasu (launched 2 May 1925, Erode; mouthpiece of the movement)
dispute: Key: Kudi Arasu (the only real journal among the options). Strictly, it was founded on 2 May 1925, not May 1924 (Wikipedia 'Kudi Arasu'); Spectrum's appendix wrongly gives 1910.

x: The resolution on Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme was passed at Karachi under Vallabhbhai Patel – in March 1931 ('1930' in the option is a misprint; no session was held in 1930).
source: Spectrum (Ahir) A Brief History of Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) pdf p.413 (Karachi session, 29 March 1931: Fundamental Rights and National Economic Programme resolutions); PMF Modern History Part 5 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-05.txt) p.797-802
evidence: PMF Part 5 p.801: no session in 1930; Karachi 1931 FR resolution
dispute: Key: Karachi (printed '1930'). Strictly, the Karachi session was held in March 1931 (Spectrum pdf p.413).

from_notes_src: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) pdf p.858
x: Gandhi presided only at Belgaum; the session was in December 1924 (the option's 1925 is a misprint), so it is still the intended answer.
source: Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) pdf p.375 (Belgaum, December 1924, the only session Gandhi presided over), p.858

from_notes: The Dandi March (12 March – 6 April 1930) reached Dandi on 5 April and culminated in breaking the salt law on 6 April 1930.
from_notes_src: PMF Modern Indian History Part 4 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-04.txt) p.190
x: The Dandi March (12 March – 6 April 1930) reached Dandi on 5 April and culminated in breaking the salt law on 6 April 1930.
source: PMF Modern Indian History Part 4 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-04.txt) p.190 (12 March – 6 April 1930; reached Dandi 5 April); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March (march 12 March – 6 April 1930; salt law broken 6 April)
dispute: Key / most books: 6 April 1930. Strictly, the marchers reached Dandi on 5 April and broke the salt law on the morning of 6 April (PMF Part 4 p.190).

x: After resigning over the Kurnool bus-routes verdict, Neelam Sanjiva Reddy joined Shastri's cabinet in 1964 as Union Minister of Steel and Mines (the 'Iron and Mines' option); he was not given Home or Finance.
source: NextGen Modern India L2 Part 13 (src/ap-history/nextgen-modern-l2-13.txt) p.2-12; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neelam_Sanjiva_Reddy ('From June 1964, Reddy was Union Minister of Steel and Mines in the Lal Bahadur Shastri government')

x: Kishanji (Mallojula Koteswara Rao, from Peddapalli) was killed by security forces in West Midnapore, West Bengal, on 24 November 2011 (the stem says 2012). Charu Majumdar died in custody in 1972, Kanu Sanyal died in 2010, Veerappan was a brigand.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kishenji (killed 24 November 2011, West Midnapore); old app notes row 264
